products.title: The Ivy Look A to Z
products.body_html:
First emerging in the Ivy League schools of America's East Coast during the 1950s and '60s, the Ivy Look has had a lasting sartorial impact on fashion and culture. Democratic, stylish, and comfortable, it has been embraced by presidents, film stars, businessmen, and hipsters alike. With its understated yet carefully curated components, the Ivy Look embodies an approachable correctness and laid-back confidence. Digging deep into the archives, this visual lexicon showcases all the Ivy essentials and how to wear them - including D for Desert Boots, L for Loafers, O for Oxford Shirts, M for Madras and T for Trenchcoats.

Each entry is accompanied by original illustrations and text by Graham Marsh alongside period album covers, magazine advertisements, movie posters and photographs of Ivy icons such as Miles Davis, Steve McQueen and Paul Newman.

products.title: Hollywood Confidential
products.body_html:
Formerly of Tatler and Vanity Fair, Dafydd Jones is a serial capturer of intimate moments during high-society functions. As famous Vanity Fair editor Graydon Carter puts it, when it comes to party photographers, "Dafydd Jones is the sniper’s sniper – the best of the best."

On numerous occasions in the 1990s and 2000s, Jones turned his lens to the faces of Hollywood with all his usual impudence, as they mingled and danced at private events in the Hollywood Hills, Oscar-night parties and awards ceremonies. The result is a rare thing – photographs that convey the underlying personalities of the world’s most public personas.

products.title: Oxford The Last Hurrah
products.body_html: Oxford: The Last Hurrah shows a world that has been written about and dramatized, yet never photographed. Affectionate and critical, it pokes affectionate fun at its subjects while celebrating English eccentricity. From the architectural marvels of the colleges to misty mornings along the river at dawn, this is Oxford at its most beautiful - and the students of the 1980s at their most raw and honest.

products.title: New York High Life / Low Life
products.body_html: At the end of the 1980s, society photographer Dafydd Jones began a new life in New York. He had been hired by Vanity Fair to attend the most talked-about parties in the city and soon found himself descending into a world of human tableaux, ladies who lunch, princesses in powder rooms and dachshunds scrapping over canapés. During the day, he captured the city streets and the ordinary citizens grounded in the real world. In these pages, the author reveals the story of New York, the highs and the lows, as the ’90s unfolded in front of his expert lens.

products.title: England The Last Hurrah
products.body_html:
Throughout the 1980s, award-winning photographer Dafydd Jones was granted access to some of England’s most exclusive upper-class events. Now, the author presents this irreverent and intimate portrait of birthday parties and charity balls, Eton picnics and private school celebrations.

With the crack of a hunting rifle and a spray of champagne, these photos give an almost cinematic account of high-society England at its most riotous and its most vulnerable. Against the backdrop of Thatcher’s Britain, globalization, the Falklands War, rising stocks and dwindling inherited fortunes, Jones reveals the inner lives of the established elite as they party long into the night-time of their fading world.

products.title: Cambridge Balls
products.body_html: Cambridge Balls is the sensational new book by bestselling social photographer Dafydd Jones. The Cambridge University colleges are renowned for many great alumni and important achievements… and also a series of marathon all-night parties, known as the May Balls, held annually to celebrate the end of the academic year. Dafydd Jones, who according to The New York Times, ‘goes about his business with cheery zest and a wicked eye’, has been granted unique access to this hidden world of revelry since 1981, during which the author of England: The Last Hurrah and Hollywood Confidential has captured an extraordinary tableau of antics and shenanigans now beautifully reproduced on these pages. From former British Prime Minister David Cameron in his Bullingdon coat to victorious rowing teams celebrating into the night, from gate crashers punting across the river to the more international student groups of modern times toasting their successes, this is a fascinating portrait of jubilation among the young, the wealthy and the academic elites of one of the world’s most famous universities.

products.title: Dark Camel Wool Cotton Textured Socks
products.body_html:
• Traditional Fair Isle
  • Cashmere Blend
  • Mid-Calf Length
  • Made in Italy

Originating on the remote Fair Isle, part of the Shetland Islands, about 100 miles off the northeastern coast of Scotland, this beautiful, intricate, and colorful folk knit style has a rich history dating back centuries. Originally prized by local fishermen for its exceptional warmth and durability, the style  gained global fame in 1921 when the Prince of Wales (later King Edward VIII) was photographed wearing a Fair Isle sweater, transforming this heritage craft into a fashion icon.  Our timeless and cozily-elegant collection of socks and sweaters honors that rich history.

products.title: Made-in-England "Old Enough to Know Better" Duke of Devonshire Sweater
products.body_html:
• 100% Scottish Lambswool
  • Embroidered "Old Enough to Know Better"
  • Made in England

Inspired by the infamous trunkful of sweaters created by the 11th Duke of Devonshire.  

The Duke, who married Deborah Mitford, the youngest of the perhaps even-more infamous Mitford sisters, commissioned a collection of sweaters with embroidered slogans that ranged from the cheeky ("Never Marry a Mitford") to the unmentionable.  Keeping in the spirit of the late Duke, we've opted for the former.

For our tribute to the Duke, we turned to FUND Knitwear whose sweaters are knitted, embroidered, and hand-finished in England from local lambswool spun by a mill on the banks of Scotland's Loch Leven.  In addition to producing beautiful knitwear, for the sale of each sweater, FUND provides 10 free school meals to children in some of the poorest countries in the world.

• Boxcloth made of 100% Wool woven in the Yorkshire Dales
  • Hand-Polished Brass Hardware
  • White Goatskin Leather Ends
  • X-back

Boxcloth, sometimes called 'buckskin', was the ultimate fabric for keeping out the cold in the 19th century. Since then, it has continued to be woven in Yorkshire.  After weaving, it is then finished by being shrunk to half its original width which tightens up the cloth, allowing it to be used for making the ultimate in classic braces.

products.title: Dark Grey Fair Isle Cashmere Socks
products.body_html:
• Traditional Fair Isle
  • Cashmere Blend
  • Mid-Calf Length
  • Made in Italy

Originating on the remote Fair Isle, part of the Shetland Islands, about 100 miles off the northeastern coast of Scotland, this beautiful, intricate, and colorful folk knit style has a rich history dating back centuries. Originally prized by local fishermen for its exceptional warmth and durability, the style  gained global fame in 1921 when the Prince of Wales (later King Edward VIII) was photographed wearing a Fair Isle sweater, transforming this heritage craft into a fashion icon.  Our timeless and cozily-elegant collection of socks and sweaters honors that rich history.

products.title: Ametora: How Japan Saved American Style - English Edition
products.body_html:
The title says it all.

As Japan rebuilt and modernized in the post-WWII years, an underground fascination with American "Aibii" (from the English word "Ivy") style took root with Japanese youth.  By 1964, these kids, dressed in shirts with strange buttoning down collars;  jackets with superfluous top buttons; and short tan pants, had acquired an official name, the "Miyuke Tribe" and, in the eyes of authorities wishing to present Japan's best face in the lead up to the 1964 Olympics, they'd become an official problem, as well.

The American-style Youth Quake had arrived in Japan and the country's fashion landscape hasn't been the same since.

In 2010, people around the fashion world rediscovered a rare 1965 Japanese photo book, Take Ivy, a documentary of student style on Ivy League campuses and one of the most influential men's style books ever published.

The craze for the book sparked the realization that the Japanese had safeguarded America's sartorial history while the US had worked to make Dress Down Friday an all-week affair.

In this seminal book, author W. David Marx makes the argument that Japanese consumers and brands have saved American fashion in both meanings of the word -- by physically archiving the clothes as canonical knowledge and protecting them from extinction through continued production-- and tells the fascinating story of how they did it.

An essential read for any student of Ivy and American Traditional ("Ametora") Style.

Originating on the remote Fair Isle, part of the Shetland Islands, about 100 miles off the northeastern coast of Scotland, this beautiful, intricate, and colorful folk knit style has a rich history dating back centuries. Originally prized by local fishermen for its exceptional warmth and durability, the style  gained global fame in 1921 when the Prince of Wales (later King Edward VIII) was photographed wearing a Fair Isle sweater, transforming this heritage craft into a fashion icon.  Our timeless and cozily-elegant collection of socks and sweaters honors that rich history.

These Trousers are Handmade-to-Order.  Please allow 4 weeks for Léo to make yours.

  • 100% Wool Donegal Tweed

  • On-Seam Pockets
  • Extended Tab Waistband
  • Zip Fly
  • Made in New York City

"Oxford Bags", the wide-legged, trouser craze of the Jazz Age originated among undergraduates at the University of Oxford around 1924. The trend reportedly began as a clever workaround to university's ban on knickerbockers, the short, baggy pants often worn for sports, when Oxford's resourceful students discovered they could easily slip these massively proportioned trousers over their athletic gear to attend lectures without violating the dress code. Representing a bold, rebellious shift away from the era's traditional slim-fit tailoring, Oxford bags quickly transcended academic life to become a hallmark of Jazz Age youth culture, gaining popularity across Europe and at American Ivy League universities throughout the mid-1920s and remaining influential into the 1950s.

products.body_html:

  • Embroidered "New York New York"
  • Made in England

Inspired by the infamous trunkful of sweaters created by the 11th Duke of Devonshire.  

The Duke, who married Deborah Mitford, the youngest of the perhaps even-more infamous Mitford sisters, commissioned a collection of sweaters with embroidered slogans that ranged from the cheeky ("Never Marry a Mitford") to the unmentionable.  Keeping in the spirit of the late Duke, we've opted for the former.

For our tribute to the Duke, we turned to FUND Knitwear whose sweaters are knitted, embroidered, and hand-finished in England from local lambswool spun by a mill on the banks of Scotland's Loch Leven.  In addition to producing beautiful knitwear, for the sale of each sweater, FUND provides 10 free school meals to children in some of the poorest countries in the world.

products.body_html:
• Classic Fit 
  • 100% Wool 
  • Crew Neck
  • Long Sleeve
  • Dry Clean Only 
  • Made in Scotland

Originating on the remote Fair Isle, part of the Shetland Islands, about 100 miles off the northeastern coast of Scotland, this beautiful, intricate, and colorful folk knit style has a rich history dating back centuries. Originally prized by local fishermen for its exceptional warmth and durability, the style  gained global fame in 1921 when the Prince of Wales (later King Edward VIII) was photographed wearing a Fair Isle sweater, transforming this heritage craft into a fashion icon.  Our timeless and cozily-elegant collection of socks and sweaters honors that rich history.

Established in 1927, this family business has produced everything from cotton underwear to traditional wool knit sweaters. products.title: Made in Canada Handknit Cowichan Sweater
products.body_html:
• Authentic Cowichan
  • Knit completely by hand in the Coast Salish region of British Columbia
  • Traditional Salmon motif
  • Trim Fit
  • 100% untreated new wool
  • Shawl collar
  • Full-zip cardigan style

Our Cowichan cardigan was knitted exclusively for us by a third-generation craftswoman from the Coast Salish region of British Columbia, Canada, historical, geographical, and cultural home of the Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest.  In our development process for this sweater, the Cowichan Tribe certified our knitter as one of the most reputable in their community.  As each sweater was knitted by one person and completely by hand, we were able to obtain only twelve pieces.  These are truly special sweaters, indeed.

With this special piece, we took pains to ensure that the sweater was the genuine article and not the commercial "Cowichan-style" knockoff many retailers sell.  To that end, we submitted our design and production plan to the Cowichan Tribes which, upon review, granted us permission to use the official registered Cowichan Sweater "APPROVED" trademark which we gratefully and proudly feature on the sweater's label.

Note: this is a substantial, handknit sweater with a trim fit.  While the knit and fit will relax slightly over time, we recommend checking the size chart and sizing up for a more traditional fit.

products.title: Vintage Dixon Ticonderoga Pencils Glass Ashtray Dish
products.body_html:
Known as “America’s Pencil,” Dixon Ticonderoga was first introduced in the early 20th century and quickly became celebrated for its quality and durability. Long favored by generations of writers, artists, and schoolchildren alike, Ticonderoga pencils also found devoted admirers among celebrated literary figures. Norman Rockwell created artwork for the company, while John Steinbeck was famously devoted to Ticonderoga pencils, sharpening them in batches as he worked on East of Eden and The Grapes of Wrath. Author Roald Dahl was also known to favor Ticonderogas during his long writing sessions.

Details: 
  • Vintage Dixon Ticonderoga Pencils glass ashtray
  • Top left corner reads: "Fort Ticonderoga, Captured by Ethan Allen May 10, 1775" in yellow
  • Center features iconic Ticonderoga pencil motif in yellow
  • Lower right corner reads: "Dixon Ticonderoga Pencils the Pencil of Progress" in yellow
  • Approximate Dimensions: 3.75" x 3.75" x 1/2"H

products.title: Vintage Gordon's Dry Gin Red Ceramic Heart Shaped Ashtray Catchall Dish
products.body_html:
Developed by Alexander Gordon in 1769, Gordon's Dry Gin has been the UK's number one gin since the late 19th-century. Gordon's was the preferred gin with the British Navy and in 1925 was awarded its first Royal Warrant by King George V.

Ernest Hemingway famously loved Gordon's, using it in his famously ice cold Montgomery Martini's with 15 parts gin to 1 part vermouth. Gordon's has been referenced in several films and novels including The Sting with Paul Newman, Alfred Hitchcock's 1929 thriller Blackmail, and Ian Fleming's 1953 debut novel Casino Royale.

Details:

products.title: Vintage The Plaza Hotel NYC Ceramic Ashtray Matchbook Holder
products.body_html:
The Plaza hotel first opened its doors in 1907 and is one of the world's finest hotels. Located on the corner of 5th Avenue and Central Park South, the hotel is at the heart of New York's premier shops and attractions. The hotel remains a New York institution and will forever be the epitome of luxury and style. 

The Plaza was a favorite of F. Scott Fitzgerald and his wife, Zelda. Fitzgerald loved the hotel so much, he even mentioned it in his most acclaimed novel, The Great Gatsby. Fitzgerald spent so much time at the Plaza that his friend, Ernest Hemingway, suggested he "leave his liver to Princeton [his alma matter] and his heart to the Plaza."

products.title: Vintage Air France Framed Luggage Label 8.5 x 8.5 in.
products.body_html:
Founded in 1933, Air France became famous for its early transatlantic flights. It became one of the first airlines to operate the supersonic Concorde in 1976. Air France is the official airline of the Cannes Film Festival.

Originally affixed to steamer trunks and suitcases, luggage labels were subtle markers of status—signaling where one had traveled and, more importantly, where one had stayed. Today, they remain among the most collectible artifacts of early luxury travel.

Details:

products.title: Vintage Belmond Hotel Splendido Portofino Mare Framed Luggage Label 8.5 x 10 in.

Portofino has long embodied a distinct vision of Mediterranean travel—discreet, sunlit, and refined. Along the Ligurian coast, it became a favored retreat for artists, aristocrats, and international society, with guests including Clark Gable, Lauren Bacall, Humphrey Bogart, Elizabeth Taylor, and Richard Burton.

Originally affixed to steamer trunks and suitcases, luggage labels were subtle markers of status—signaling where one had traveled and, more importantly, where one had stayed. Today, they remain among the most collectible artifacts of early luxury travel.

Details:

products.title: UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA SILK PAPERWEIGHT
products.body_html:
From 1910-1915, the American Tobacco Company offered small silk collegiate banners as an incentive premium in packages of Egyptienne Luxury Cigarettes. The series contained 150 colleges and universities with each silk containing the school's seal or coat-of-arms with its name below. Beautifully encased in a glass paperweight, these rare and colorful collector’s items make a great gift for students and graduates alike.

Each silk measures approximately 1 ¾” x 3 ¼” and is mounted on a base of blue striped oxford cloth fabric. Choose from 40 schools shown. 

Bear in mind, the silks are antiques, so some variance in color and shape is to be expected.

Please allow up to 2 weeks to ship. As these items are made to order, they are considered to be final sale.

The Yale Bulldogs Baseball team were winners of the Eastern Intercollegiate Baseball League Championship (EIBL) in 1948, the de-facto Ivy League conference from 1930-1992. This league also included the collegiate athletics stalwarts Army and Navy. 

The squad advanced to the College World Series that year, led by captain and third-baseman (and J. Press customer), George H. W. Bush.

This jersey pays homage to that championship team from 1948, made with genuine baseball flannel and finished with authentic felt lettering.

THE 1949 SEALS BALLCAP THAT TOURED POST-WAR JAPAN

A charter member of the famed Pacific Coast League, the San Francisco Seals are one of the most recognizable minor league teams of all time. In 1949, as part of a diplomatic mission requested by the U.S. government, the team went on a historic post-war tour of Japan led by their manager Lefty O’Doul — a man who contributed greatly to the popularity of baseball in Japan, before and after the war. Over half a million fans came out to watch the Seals play, including the Emperor himself, leading General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers in Japan, to call it, “the greatest piece of diplomacy ever.”

This is a recreation of the ballcap worn by the San Francisco Seals in 1949, featuring genuine navy wool broadcloth and felt lettering, just like the one they wore on their history-making tour.

products.title: Black Ivy: A Revolt in Style
products.body_html:
Black Ivy: A Revolt in Style charts a period in American history when Black men across the country —from the most avant-garde jazz musicians, visual artists and poets to architects, philosophers and writers— adopted the clothing of a privileged elite and made it their own. Author Jason Jules styles it a “sartorial power grab.” Boasting the work of some of America's finest photographers and image-makers, "Black Ivy" chronicles how a generation of men took the classic Ivy Look and made it cool, edgy, and unpredictable in ways that continue to influence today's modern menswear.

Hardcover

Classic looks. Modern comfort.

products.title: Easy on the Ivy: Japan Edition
products.body_html:
Easy On The Ivy: Japan Edition by Tom Hoy is a complementary 'zine to Tom's popular "Easy On the Ivy" Substack which explores the heritage, culture and global influence of Ivy
League style through deep dives, interviews and personal reflections  "Easy on the Ivy: Japan Edition" sits alongside it as a physical extension of that same world.

When Tom visited Japan for the first time, the trip felt too special to keep purely digital and so the idea for the physical 'zine was born.  

The zine is anecdotal, sharing Tom’s trip through words, photos and the stories to explore the relationship between American Ivy style and its reinterpretation there. The tone is informed but personal, aimed at readers who genuinely care about the history and ongoing relevance of the style.

products.title: Rolex Domino's Air-King 14000 Full Set w/ Hangtag Unpolished
products.body_html:
The Rolex-Domino’s connection is perhaps the ultimate high-low collaboration. These watches were not made for purchase by the public, but as a way to reward Domino’s franchise owners who hit their sales targets.

All these watches were originally ordered through Schlanderer and Sons in Ann Arbor, Michigan, where Domino’s has its headquarters. In the past, these watches on the secondhand market were generally the least expensive Rolex a person could purchase as few people wanted a pizza logo like this on their dial. Dealers would buy them, swap out the Domino’s dial, and polish off the case back initials. Over the last year, however, they have gained a massive following. The watch features an engraving on the back with the recipient’s initials.

You can learn about these watches in our video Collector Conversation: Tom Monaghan - Founder of Domino's Pizza - on the Domino's Rolex.

This version features the “tilted logo” that is the last version of Dominos’s Rolex watch with the logo on the dial. .

The watch features a U^ serial dating to 1997. The case appears to be unpolished.

The watch comes as a “full set” with a box, papers and hangtag. It was originally sold in 1998. We do not know the full service history, but it is running well. It recently passed a water resistance test of 5 bar. 

To learn more about Rolex-Domino’s story, watch the video ”Rolex Model NEVER in Stores”.

products.title: Illustrated Ivy
products.body_html:
Illustrated Ivy is an overview of Ivy League style depicted in a series of endearing, impeccably detailed illustrations by Kazuo Hozumi. Since their 1963 debut in the Japanese magazine Men’s Club, Hozumi’s cheerful Ivy boys and girls have acted as guides to shifting styles within the pantheon of Ivy League clothing. In addition to cataloguing a subtly evolving style of dress, Hozumi has gathered a cult following for his beguiling, deceptively simple approach.

Illustrated Ivy is the first time Kazuo Hozumi’s Ivy illustrations have been available with his accompanying text in English.

products.title: Ametora: How Japan Saved American Style - Japanese Edition
products.body_html:
As Japan rebuilt and modernized in the post-WWII years, an underground fascination with American "Aibii" (from the English word "Ivy") style took root with Japanese youth.  By 1964, these kids, dressed in shirts with strange buttoning collars;  jackets with superfluous top buttons; and short tan pants, had acquired an official name, the "Miyuke Tribe" and, in the eyes of authorities wishing to present Japan's best face in the lead up to the 1964 Olympics, they'd become an official problem, as well. The American-style Youth Quake had arrived in Japan and the country's fashion landscape hasn't been the same since.

In 2010, the fashion world rediscovered a rare 1965 Japanese photo book, Take Ivy, a documentary of student style on Ivy League campuses and one of the most influential men's style books ever published. The craze for the book sparked the realization that the Japanese had safeguarded America's sartorial history while the US had worked to make Dress Down Friday an all-week affair.

In this seminal book, author W. David Marx makes the argument that Japanese consumers and brands have saved American fashion in both meanings of the word - by physically archiving the clothes as canonical knowledge and protecting them from extinction through continued production-- and tells the fascinating story of how they did it.

An essential read for any student of Ivy and American Traditional ("Ametora") Style.

1985. Ginza Kabuki Theatre. Tokyo.

The vivid orange, green, and black stripes running vertically from floor to ceiling.

Like a great big kimono, waiting to open up and reveal the secrets of kabuki to you.

The low murmur of the audience is silenced by the sharp cracks of wooden clappers. The show is about to begin.

The beat of the drums and the plucking of the shamisen, slowly picking up speed into a expansive roar with the applause, while the curtain remains placid. 

Then the swell of energy is split. 

The curtain is quickly drawn back, transporting you back to the age where honor meant something and justice was delivered with a katana.

products.body_html:

  • 2 1/2" width

1958. Shochiku Studio. Tokyo. 

The famed film director Yasujiro Ozu is working on his first color film, Equinox Flower. It would feature what would go on to become as famous as the other actors in his films, the red kettle. 

The red kettle that Ozu himself went to pick out and buy. The kettle that the director loved so much, he took it home after production was finished. 

Ozu’s signature camera position was low on the floor, to put you on the tatami floor with the characters. To the man for whom visual composition was practically another character, every little piece had significance. 

And there it is, the red kettle, placed lovingly by the director to radiate its bright warmth from its little corner.

products.title: Made-in-Japan Daruma Whiskey Club Tie
products.body_html:
• 100% Silk Woven in Kyoto
  • 2 1/2" width
  • Handsewn
  • Made in Japan

1980. Bar in downtown Kyoto. 

Coming in from the rain, you don’t know this place, but you’re just glad it’s dry. You peel off your wet trenchcoat and look down the bar to see if there’s anything worth drinking. 

Right now you don’t really care what you’re drinking, you’re just waiting for someone. But of course you care.

Then you see it, a brown bulb beaming in the shadowy bar. The classic Japanese whiskey in that round bottle, nicknamed “the Daruma.” 

That first sip gets you warm, the second sip gets you thinking.

Maybe being kept waiting isn’t so bad after all.

products.title: Thirty Years On! A Private View of Public Schools
products.body_html:
The British public school system has, for centuries, been the envy of the civilized world. Not only for its high standards of education, but also for its unyielding propensity for producing Empire builders and leaders in the fields of politics, science, economics, sport and the arts.

Over the course of centuries, public schools have accumulated a bewildering array of quirky traditions. With the possible exception of the Church, no institutions so fervently hold onto their rituals, customs and costumes as the public schools, be it the Tudor uniforms of Christ's Hospital, the straw hats of Harrow, or the Eton Wall Game and Winchester College football.

In the late 1980s, photographer Mark Draisey was given privileged access to these usually closed and private worlds to produce a stunning record of life inside institutions that were, as a rule, out of bounds to the majority of the population. This collection was taken at a time just prior to major changes in the boarding house conditions and the general modernisation of facilities at many of the schools, brought about by a more competitive market, plus the introduction of girls into these once male-dominated institutions.

This supremely evocative collection is a unique insight into the life within twenty-five of Britain's leading boy's public schools just before they changed forever. Images of austere dormitories and bleak bathrooms, beagling on the moors and Sunday Chapel, cadet training and early morning rowing, will remind thousands of spartan but more certain times when tradition and eccentricity mingled with educational excellence to produce generations of boys destined to succeed.

Schools featured include: Ampleforth College; Charterhouse; Christ's Hospital School; Clifton College; Eton College; Fettes College; Haileybury; Harrow School; Hurstpierpoint College; The King's School, Canterbury; Lancing College; Loretto School; Marlborough College; Monmouth School; Pangbourne College; Radley College; Repton School; Rugby School; Sedbergh School; Sherborne School; Shrewsbury School; Stowe School; Wellington College; Westminster School; Winchester College.

Only NY × J. Press pays homage to New York’s special ability to bring people together from all walks of life: the city’s way of facilitating the exchange and flow of ideas, styles, and inspiration among people and institutions who, in any other city, might never cross paths.

J. Press is a venerable institution in the city. While the business was established up the coast in New Haven in 1902, founder Jacobi Press came to New York City for fitting appointments every Wednesday for over a decade, before opening J. Press’ original New York store in 1919. Only NY is an independent lifestyle brand inspired by the city, the outdoors, and the arts since 2007. An official marquee licensee of the City of New York and the MTA for over a decade, Only NY is known for a considered and honest approach in apparel, accessories, and home goods that represent New York on the global stage.

This collection bridges tailored and casual through a shared appreciation for classic American sportswear. Built around the palette of the New York City flag, the capsule blends J. Press’ Ivy League tradition with Only NY’s hyper-local illustrative approach.

ABOUT OUR VINTAGE PENNANTS

Felt college pennants began being made in the early 1900s with the rise of collegiate sports (more specifically, this new sport called football!) in the United States. Given out at special games, events, and venues, our preserved vintage pennants come to you from important moments in your school or team’s history.

We have traveled the country finding rare and one of a kind vintage pennants that capture your memories and the memories of the past. Each pennant has its own unique character and story. Perfect for entering freshmen, recent graduates, older alumni, and more!

*Note: Placement of pennant in the frame can vary slightly upon framing.
